title: What fraction of the workforce does research?
text:
Source: OECD, Main Science and Technology Indicators (MSTI), dataflow DSD_MSTI@DF_MSTI.

Data accessed: September 29, 2026, via the OECD SDMX API.

Population: 1981 - 2024; 45 countries and economies (OECD members plus partners such as China, Taiwan, Singapore and Russia), and the OECD and EU27 totals.
Economic growth ultimately depends on the discovery of new ideas: better technologies, medicines, production methods, and ways of organizing economic activity all raise the standard of living. So where do “new ideas” come from, exactly? In the words of Joel Mokyr:
At risk of stating the obvious: new ideas are produced through the time and effort of people engaged in research. But this straightforward relationship becomes much more complicated when you try to do measurement - what exactly do we mean by “new ideas” and “research effort”?
The stock of economically useful ideas cannot be observed directly (how would one go about measuring an “idea”?) Growth accounting therefore often treats growth in total factor productivity (TFP)—a summary measure of how effectively an economy transforms measured inputs into output—as a first-order proxy for growth in productive knowledge. TFP is not, of course, the same thing as “knowledge” or “ideas” in the ordinary sense, but there are good reasons to use it as a measure of productive knowledge (that discussion is beyond the scope of this article).
Jones (2022) provides a simple and transparent growth-accounting framework that captures the sentiment of Mokyr’s quotation. Intuitively, the following equation shows that the flow of new ideas depends on growth in the total labor force and in the fraction of workers who do research. Roughly speaking, if we have more people, and if a greater fraction of them are working on research, we should get more ideas. \(\text{TFP}\) is the empirical proxy for “new ideas”; \(L\) and \(s\) are direct measurements of the size of the labor force and the fraction of the labor force working in the research sector (respectively).
\[
\underbrace{d\log \text{TFP}_t}_\text{growth in new ideas}
=
\underbrace{\gamma d\log L_t}_\text{growth in the labor force} +
\underbrace{\gamma d\log s_t}_\text{growth in the fraction of \\ the labor force doing research}
+ \quad \text{other terms}
\tag{1}\]
The important subtlety is that this equation relates the growth rates of these quantities, not their levels. TFP growth depends partly on (i) the growth rate of the labor force, \(d \log L_t\), and (ii) the growth rate of research intensity, \(d \log s_t\) — that is, the rate at which the share of the labor force engaged in research increases. Even if research intensity remains constant, total research effort can grow as the labor force expands. Conversely, a country with a stable labor force can increase its research effort by devoting a rising share of its workers to research.
Hopefully this simple introduction provides sufficient motivation for the central topic of this article - measuring the fraction of the workforce that does research \((s)\), and seeing how that number has been trending over time.

section: Reading and cleaning the raw file
text:
Reading and cleaning the raw file
The raw OECD file has 27,330 rows. It covers six measures, several units each (full-time equivalents, headcount, percentages and per-1,000 ratios), and year-over-year growth rates. I keep only the levels (not growth rates), drop blank cells, and use the OECD’s own metadata file to turn codes such as KOR and E into readable labels.






NoteCode: loading labels from the OECD’s metadata





def load_labels() -> dict[str, dict[str, str]]:
    """Read human-readable names for every code from the OECD's own metadata.

    The data file only contains codes such as "KOR" or "E". The structure file
    maps each code to its label (e.g. "Korea", "Estimated value"). We use the
    OECD's labels rather than typing our own so they cannot drift or be misspelled.
    Returns {codelist id: {code: label}}, e.g. labels["CL_AREA"]["KOR"] == "Korea".
    """
    structure = json.loads(RAW_STRUCTURE.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    labels = {}
    for codelist in structure["data"]["codelists"]:
        labels[codelist["id"]] = {code["id"]: code["name"] for code in codelist["codes"]}
    # The one label we replace: the OECD's "Chinese Taipei" is shown as "Taiwan",
    # the name most English-language readers know.
    labels["CL_AREA"]["TWN"] = "Taiwan"
    return labels









NoteCode: loading and filtering observations





def load_observations() -> dict[tuple[str, str, str, int], dict[str, str]]:
    """Read the raw OECD CSV and index the rows we need.

    The raw file contains every unit and transformation the OECD publishes for
    our six measures, including year-over-year growth rates. We keep only the
    levels (TRANSFORMATION "_Z" = "not applicable", i.e. no transformation) and
    only rows that actually contain a number.

    Returns a dictionary keyed by (country, measure, unit, year) so that later
    steps can look up, say, Korea's researchers in FTE for 2024 directly.
    """
    with RAW_DATA.open(encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as source:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(source))

    indexed = {}
    for row in rows:
        if row["TRANSFORMATION"] != "_Z":   # drop growth-rate and index rows
            continue
        if row["OBS_VALUE"] == "":          # drop empty cells (no value reported)
            continue
        if row["FREQ"] != "A":              # we asked for annual; enforce it
            raise ValueError(f"Unexpected frequency {row['FREQ']!r}")

        key = (row["REF_AREA"], row["MEASURE"], row["UNIT_MEASURE"], int(row["TIME_PERIOD"]))
        if key in indexed:
            # Two values for the same country/measure/unit/year would make the
            # result depend on file order. Stop rather than silently pick one.
            raise ValueError(f"Duplicate observation for {key}")
        indexed[key] = row
    return indexed


def value(row: dict[str, str]) -> float:
    """Return an observation's numeric value in plain units.

    UNIT_MULT is a power of ten: total employment is published in thousands
    (UNIT_MULT = 3), so 103399 means 103,399,000 people. Everything else in
    this investigation has UNIT_MULT = 0.
    """
    return float(row["OBS_VALUE"]) * 10 ** int(row["UNIT_MULT"] or 0)



The OECD tags many values with status flags, such as estimated, provisional, definition differs or break in series. These flags are kept rather than dropped. They appear in every chart tooltip and in the downloadable tables.






NoteCode: translating status flags into words





def describe_flags(row: dict[str, str], labels: dict[str, dict[str, str]]) -> str:
    """Translate an observation's status codes into readable words.

    The OECD attaches up to three status codes (e.g. "E" = estimated,
    "B" = break in series, "P" = provisional, "D" = definition differs) plus an
    auxiliary code (e.g. "M2" = underestimated). We keep all of them, in words,
    so readers can see them in chart tooltips and the downloadable tables.
    """
    notes = []
    for column in ("OBS_STATUS", "OBS_STATUS_2", "OBS_STATUS_3"):
        code = row.get(column, "")
        if code and code != "A":  # "A" means "normal value": nothing to report
            notes.append(labels["CL_OBS_STATUS"].get(code, code))
    aux = row.get("AUX_OBS_STATUS", "")
    if aux:
        notes.append(labels["CL_AUX_OBS_STATUS"].get(aux, aux))
    # Remove repeats while keeping order (the same code can appear twice).
    return "; ".join(dict.fromkeys(notes))


def has_break(row: dict[str, str]) -> bool:
    """True if the OECD marks this year as a break in the series.

    A break means the method or definition changed, so the jump between this
    year and the previous one may be partly an artefact of measurement.
    """
    codes = {row.get(c, "") for c in ("OBS_STATUS", "OBS_STATUS_2", "OBS_STATUS_3")}
    return "B" in codes or row.get("AUX_OBS_STATUS") == "A2"

title: What fraction of the workforce does research?
text:
Coverage
MSTI is not a world dataset. It has researcher shares for 45 countries and economies: every OECD member except Colombia, plus eight partners (Bulgaria, China, Taiwan, Croatia, Romania, Russia, Singapore and South Africa). In 2023, the ones that report employment employed about 1.4 billion people. That is roughly 40% of the world’s approximately 3.4 billion employed people. Several of the world’s largest labor forces are not covered at all, including India, Indonesia, Brazil, Nigeria, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
The aggregate series below uses a narrower group. To avoid jumps when countries enter or leave the data, it keeps only the 23 countries that report every year from 1995 to 2023 (the decision is explained in full below). That drops some large MSTI countries, such as Mexico, the United Kingdom, Australia and Taiwan, whose series are too short, stale or patchy.
In 2023, the panel’s 23 countries employed about 1.25 billion people in total. Of those, about 8.2 million full-time equivalents were researchers. China alone accounts for 740 million of the panel’s workers (59%), so the pooled numbers are heavily weighted toward China.






ImportantLimitation: coverage of the data



The panel’s 23 countries employ about 1.2 billion people in total. Most of the world outside the OECD and its partners is not in MSTI at all.

title: What fraction of the workforce does research?
text:
Trends
The first question is the simplest: across all the countries in the data, what share of the combined workforce does research, and how fast is that share growing? For each year I add up full-time-equivalent researchers across countries and divide by the countries’ combined employment. This weights each country by the size of its workforce, so it is the share of the pooled labor force, \(s\) in Equation 1, not an average of country shares.






WarningData Processing Decision: a fixed panel of countries



Countries enter the data in different years, and some report only every other year. Summing over whoever happens to report would make the total jump each time a country appears or disappears. So the aggregate uses only the 23 countries that report researchers in every year from 1995 to 2023: Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, China (People’s Republic of), Czechia, Germany, Spain, France, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Korea, Latvia, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Singapore, Slovak Republic, Slovenia, Türkiye, United States. Countries that report every other year (such as Sweden, Norway and Austria) and those with short or stale series (such as the United Kingdom and Australia) are left out.



The China problem
China accounts for 59% of this panel’s employment (in 2023), so whatever happens to China’s numbers dominates the pooled total. Before 2009, China did not count researchers the way the other countries do. The international definition of a researcher comes from the OECD’s Frascati Manual. Before 2009, China counted UNESCO’s “scientists and engineers”, a broader group. The OECD therefore marks every Chinese value before 2009 as definition differs and marks 2009 as a break in series.
You can see the change in the data. China’s published figure falls by -32.7% (in log terms) from 2008 to 2009, the only large fall anywhere in its series. Left alone, this would show up as a collapse in the pooled series, and it would make every pre-2009 level too high relative to later years.






WarningData Processing Decision: level-shifting China’s pre-2009 figures



To put China’s earlier years on the Frascati basis, I multiply every Chinese researcher count before 2009 by one constant factor. This is a level shift: it moves the whole pre-2009 series down by the same proportion and leaves its year-to-year growth rates unchanged. China’s employment figures have no break, so they are not touched, and no other country is adjusted.
The size of the shift is the 2008-to-2009 change that is due to the definition alone. The observed change also contains a year of genuine change, so that part is subtracted out. I assume it equals China’s average growth in the years either side of the break. All figures are changes in the natural log of researchers per 1,000 employed, in percent:








Step
Calculation
Value




Observed change, 2008 → 2009
from the data
-32.7%


Growth the year before, 2007 → 2008
from the data
10.9%


Growth the year after, 2009 → 2010
from the data
4.6%


Assumed genuine change, 2008 → 2009
average of the two rows above
7.7%


Step due to the definition change
observed − assumed genuine
-40.4%


Factor applied to pre-2009 counts
\(e^{\text{step}}\)
0.667



So China’s researcher counts for 1995–2008 are reduced by about 33%. After the shift, China’s growth from 2008 to 2009 is exactly the assumed 7.7%.
The main alternative is to treat the whole observed change as the definition step. That would assume China’s research share did not grow at all in 2009, which is implausible for a series growing 4.6–10.9% a year either side of the break. The adjustment is an estimate: the OECD does not publish an overlap year with both definitions, so the true size of the step is unknown.




The aggregate series
The chart shows three lines and the adjustment:

(i) 22 countries excluding China: the pooled share for every panel country except China. No adjustment is involved.
(ii) China, exactly as published. The line is broken between 2008 and 2009, where the definition changes. The dashed line is China’s pre-2009 series after the level shift, on the Frascati basis.
(iii) All 23 countries, including China, using China’s level-shifted figures before 2009. This is the headline series.



Show the aggregate level chart code

// Series names, in the order analyze.py writes them.

chinaName = aggSeries[1]

allName = aggSeries[3]

// Direct labels at the right-hand end of the three main lines.
aggLast = [exChinaName, chinaName, allName]

Plot.plot({

  height: 420,
  marginRight: 140,
  x: {label: null, tickFormat: d => String(d)},
  y: {grid: true, zero: true, label: "↑ Researchers (FTE) per 1,000 employed"},
  marks: [

    // Where China switches to the Frascati definition.

      text: () => "China adopts the\nFrascati definition", fill: "currentColor", fillOpacity: 0.7
    }),

    Plot.line(aggregate.filter(d => d.series === exChinaName || d.series === allName), {
      x: "year", y: "researchers_per_1000", z: "series", stroke: d => aggColor.get(d.series), strokeWidth: 2.5
    }),
    // (ii) China as published: z splits the line by definition, so there is a gap at the break.
    Plot.line(aggregate.filter(d => d.series === chinaName), {
      x: "year", y: "researchers_per_1000", z: "china_definition", stroke: chinaColor, strokeWidth: 2.5
    }),
    // China before the break, after the level shift.
    Plot.line(aggregate.filter(d => d.series === chinaShiftedName), {
      x: "year", y: "researchers_per_1000", stroke: chinaColor, strokeWidth: 1.75, strokeDasharray: "5,4"
    }),
    Plot.text([chinaShiftedEnd], {
      x: "year", y: "researchers_per_1000", text: () => "China, level-shifted",
      dx: -4, dy: 12, textAnchor: "end", fill: chinaColor, fontSize: 11
    }),
    Plot.text(aggLast, {
      x: "year", y: "researchers_per_1000", text: "label",
      dx: 6, textAnchor: "start", fill: d => aggColor.get(d.series), fontWeight: 600
    }),
    Plot.tip(aggregate, Plot.pointer({
      x: "year", y: "researchers_per_1000", stroke: d => aggColor.get(d.series),
      title: d => [
        `${d.series}, ${d.year}`,
        `${d.researchers_per_1000.toFixed(2)} researchers per 1,000 employed (${(d.researchers_per_1000 / 10).toFixed(2)}% of workforce)`,
        `${(d.researchers_fte / 1e6).toFixed(2)} million researchers / ${(d.employment / 1e6).toFixed(0)} million employed`,
        d.china_shifted ? "China's researcher count level-shifted to the Frascati basis" : "",
        d.breaks ? `Break in series: ${d.breaks}` : ""
      ].filter(Boolean).join("\n")
    }))
  ]
})








































































Across all 23 countries, with China level-shifted, the share of workers doing research rose from 2.5 per 1,000 in 1995 to 6.6 per 1,000 in 2023, an average growth rate of 3.5% a year. Without China, the level is higher but growth is slower: from 5.8 to 10.3 per 1,000, or 2.1% a year. China’s share of workers in research is still well below the rest of the panel’s, but it is rising much faster. Because China has so many workers, that pulls the pooled growth rate up.


The growth rate
The second chart shows the year-to-year growth rate of series (iii), \(d \log s_t\), the term that enters Equation 1. The thin line is the raw annual change, \(100 \times (\ln s_t - \ln s_{t-1})\). Raw annual changes are noisy: they pick up series breaks, recessions and swings in employment. The thick line is the trend growth rate from a Hodrick-Prescott (HP) filter.






WarningData Processing Decision: smoothing the growth rate



The HP filter fits a smooth trend through \(\ln s_t\), trading off closeness to the data against how sharply the trend is allowed to bend. The thick line is the year-to-year change in that trend. How smooth the trend is depends on one parameter, \(\lambda\). I use \(\lambda = 6.25\), the standard value for annual data (Ravn and Uhlig, 2002); it is the annual equivalent of the standard 1,600 for quarterly data. Like any two-sided filter, the HP trend is least reliable at the start and end of the sample, so the first and last few years of the trend should be read cautiously.




Show the growth-rate chart code
growth = aggregate.filter(d => d.series === allName && d.growth_pct != null)
growthColor = aggColor.get(allName)
signed = v => `${v >= 0 ? "+" : ""}${v.toFixed(1)}%`
growthEnd = growth[growth.length - 1]

Plot.plot({
  width,
  height: 340,
  marginRight: 90,

    Plot.dot(growth, {x: "year", y: "growth_pct", fill: growthColor, fillOpacity: 0.6, r: 2.5}),

    Plot.text([growthEnd], {x: "year", y: "trend_growth_pct", text: () => "HP trend", dx: 8, textAnchor: "start", fill: growthColor, fontWeight: 600}),

    }))

})











































NoteCode: building the aggregate series and China’s level shift





def china_level_shift(obs) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Estimate the definitional step in China's series at BREAK_YEAR (DECISION 5).

    All changes are in natural logs of researchers per 1,000 employed:

        observed     = ln s(2009) - ln s(2008)          the jump in the data
        underlying   = average of ln s(2008) - ln s(2007)
                       and        ln s(2010) - ln s(2009)  assumed real change
        step         = observed - underlying             the change of definition
        factor       = exp(step)                          multiply pre-2009 counts by this
    """
    def log_ratio(year):
        return math.log(value(obs[(BREAK_COUNTRY, "T_RS", "10P3EMP", year)]))

    y = BREAK_YEAR
    observed = log_ratio(y) - log_ratio(y - 1)
    before = log_ratio(y - 1) - log_ratio(y - 2)
    after = log_ratio(y + 1) - log_ratio(y)
    underlying = (before + after) / 2
    step = observed - underlying
    return {
        "observed": observed, "before": before, "after": after,
        "underlying": underlying, "step": step, "factor": math.exp(step),
    }


def build_aggregate(obs, labels) -> tuple[list[dict[str, object]], list[str], dict[str, float]]:
    """The share of all employed people who are researchers, pooled across countries.

    For each year, add up full-time-equivalent researchers across a group of
    countries and divide by the group's total employment:

        share_t = sum of researchers (FTE) / sum of employment x 1,000

    This weights each country by its workforce, so it is the share of the
    *combined* labor force doing research, not an average of country shares.

    Four series are written:
      - the panel (DECISION 4) excluding China;
      - China alone, exactly as published (the break is left in);
      - China's pre-2009 years after the level shift (DECISION 5), to show
        the adjustment;
      - the whole panel including China, with China's pre-2009 researcher
        counts level-shifted. This is the headline series.

    For the two pooled series, the growth rate is the change in the natural
    log, d log s in the equation above, in percent: 100 x (ln share_t -
    ln share_t-1). The trend growth rate applies the HP filter (DECISION 6)
    to ln share and takes the year-to-year change in that trend.
    Each year also lists the countries the OECD flags with a break in series.
    """
    years = range(AGGREGATE_START, AGGREGATE_END + 1)
    panel = sorted(
        area for area in {a for (a, m, u, y) in obs if m == "T_RS" and u == "FTE"}
        if area not in AGGREGATES
        and all((area, "T_RS", "FTE", y) in obs and (area, "TOT_EMP", "PS", y) in obs for y in years)
    )
    shift = china_level_shift(obs)
    china = labels["CL_AREA"][BREAK_COUNTRY].split(" (")[0]   # "China"

    def researchers(area, year, adjust):
        count = value(obs[(area, "T_RS", "FTE", year)])
        if adjust and area == BREAK_COUNTRY and year < BREAK_YEAR:
            count *= shift["factor"]
        return count

    groups = [
        # (series name, member countries, apply China level shift?, years, compute growth?)
        (f"{len(panel) - 1} countries excluding {china}",
         [a for a in panel if a != BREAK_COUNTRY], False, years, True),
        (f"{china} (as published)", [BREAK_COUNTRY], False, years, False),
        (f"{china}, pre-{BREAK_YEAR} level-shifted", [BREAK_COUNTRY], True,
         range(AGGREGATE_START, BREAK_YEAR), False),
        (f"All {len(panel)} countries ({china} level-shifted)", panel, True, years, True),
    ]

    table = []
    for series, members, adjust, span, with_growth in groups:
        fte = [sum(researchers(a, y, adjust) for a in members) for y in span]
        employment = [sum(value(obs[(a, "TOT_EMP", "PS", y)]) for a in members) for y in span]
        log_share = [math.log(r / e * 1000) for r, e in zip(fte, employment)]
        log_trend = hp_trend(log_share, HP_SMOOTHING) if with_growth else None
        for i, year in enumerate(span):
            breaks = [
                labels["CL_AREA"].get(a, a) for a in members
                if has_break(obs[(a, "T_RS", "10P3EMP", year)])
            ]
            table.append({
                "series": series,
                "year": year,
                "countries": len(members),
                "researchers_fte": round(fte[i]),
                "employment": round(employment[i]),
                "researchers_per_1000": round(math.exp(log_share[i]), 4),
                # True where China's count has been multiplied by the shift factor.
                "china_shifted": adjust and BREAK_COUNTRY in members and year < BREAK_YEAR,
                # Which side of China's definition change this year is on;
                # the chart uses it to leave a gap in China's published line.
                "china_definition": "Frascati" if year >= BREAK_YEAR else "pre-Frascati",
                "growth_pct": round(100 * (log_share[i] - log_share[i - 1]), 3)
                              if with_growth and i else "",
                "trend_growth_pct": round(100 * (log_trend[i] - log_trend[i - 1]), 3)
                                    if with_growth and i else "",
                "breaks": "; ".join(breaks),
            })
    return table, [labels["CL_AREA"].get(a, a) for a in panel], shift
The HP filter, written out so it needs no numerical library (it matches statsmodels’ hpfilter to about 10⁻¹⁵):
def hp_trend(series: list[float], smoothing: float) -> list[float]:
    """Hodrick-Prescott trend of a series.

    The trend t minimises
        sum (y - t)^2  +  smoothing x sum (second difference of t)^2,
    i.e. it stays close to the data but is penalised for changing direction.
    The minimum solves the linear system (I + smoothing x D'D) t = y, where D
    takes second differences. We build that small matrix and solve it by
    Gaussian elimination, so no numerical library is needed.
    """
    n = len(series)
    # D'D for second differences, written out directly.
    matrix = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    for i in range(n - 2):
        weights = {i: 1.0, i + 1: -2.0, i + 2: 1.0}
        for r, wr in weights.items():
            for c, wc in weights.items():
                matrix[r][c] += smoothing * wr * wc
    for i in range(n):
        matrix[i][i] += 1.0

    # Gaussian elimination. The matrix is symmetric positive definite, so no
    # pivoting is needed.
    rhs = list(series)
    for col in range(n):
        for row in range(col + 1, n):
            factor = matrix[row][col] / matrix[col][col]
            if factor:
                for k in range(col, n):
                    matrix[row][k] -= factor * matrix[col][k]
                rhs[row] -= factor * rhs[col]
    trend = [0.0] * n
    for row in reversed(range(n)):
        known = sum(matrix[row][k] * trend[k] for k in range(row + 1, n))
        trend[row] = (rhs[row] - known) / matrix[row][row]
    return trend





Trends by country
I now plot the series for each country separately. Hollow circles mark years the OECD flags as a break in series. At a break, the method or coverage changed, so part of the jump may be an artefact of measurement. China’s values before 2009 are shown level-shifted to the Frascati basis, as in the aggregate series above (multiplied by 0.667), so its line has no artificial drop at 2009. The tooltips give the published figure alongside. No other country is adjusted.

Three main patterns stand out to me:

South Korea’s researcher share has grown very fast. Between 2000 and 2024, South Korea more than tripled its researcher share (from about 5 to 17.6 per 1,000), moving from the middle of the OECD to the top.
Most of Europe and the United States rose steadily.
Japan has been flat for more than twenty years, at about 10 per 1,000. It was one of the leaders in 2000 and is now close to the OECD average.







NoteCode: building the country-year table





def build_timeseries(obs, labels) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    """One row per country-year with both headline ratios side by side.

    - researchers_per_1000:  T_RS, researchers only
    - rd_personnel_per_1000: T_TT, researchers + technicians + support staff
    A year appears if at least one of the two ratios is published for it; the
    other is left blank rather than filled in or interpolated.

    researchers_per_1000_adjusted is the same as researchers_per_1000 except
    for China before BREAK_YEAR, where it applies the level shift from
    DECISION 5 (see china_level_shift). The trend chart uses this column; the
    rankings use the published figures, which are unaffected because every
    country's latest year is after the break.
    """
    shift = china_level_shift(obs)
    country_years = {
        (area, year)
        for (area, measure, unit, year) in obs
        if unit == "10P3EMP" and measure in ("T_RS", "T_TT")
    }
    table = []
    for area, year in sorted(country_years):
        researchers = obs.get((area, "T_RS", "10P3EMP", year))
        personnel = obs.get((area, "T_TT", "10P3EMP", year))
        shifted = bool(researchers) and area == BREAK_COUNTRY and year < BREAK_YEAR
        table.append({
            "country_code": area,
            "country": labels["CL_AREA"].get(area, area),
            "is_aggregate": area in AGGREGATES,
            "year": year,
            "researchers_per_1000": round(value(researchers), 4) if researchers else "",
            "rd_personnel_per_1000": round(value(personnel), 4) if personnel else "",
            "researchers_flags": describe_flags(researchers, labels) if researchers else "",
            "rd_personnel_flags": describe_flags(personnel, labels) if personnel else "",
            "researchers_break": has_break(researchers) if researchers else "",
            "researchers_per_1000_adjusted": (
                round(value(researchers) * (shift["factor"] if shifted else 1), 4)
                if researchers else ""
            ),
            "researchers_shifted": shifted,
        })
    return table









ImportantIssue: gaps and breaks



Some countries reported only every other year in earlier decades. The chart draws straight lines across those gaps; it does not fill in values.

title: What fraction of the workforce does research?
text:
Rankings
The ranking rests on three analytical choices (decisions 1-3 below; decisions 4-6 belong to the aggregate trend). They are all named constants at the top of analyze.py:






NoteCode: the analytical decisions, as constants





# DECISION 1: Which years count as "current"?
# Countries report on different schedules. A country whose latest figure is
# many years old would be ranked against others' recent figures, which is
# misleading in a field that has grown quickly. We keep a country in the
# current rankings only if its latest value is within this many years of the
# most recent year anyone reports. Stale countries are listed, not hidden.
CURRENT_WINDOW_YEARS = 5

# DECISION 2: Which rows are regional aggregates rather than countries?
# They are kept in the data for comparison but drawn differently in charts
# and never counted as a "country" in the text.
AGGREGATES = {"OECD", "EU27_2020"}

# DECISION 3: How closely must our recomputation match the OECD's figure?
# The OECD publishes the ratio to ~10 significant digits, so any real
# discrepancy would be far larger than one part in a million.
RATIO_TOLERANCE = 1e-6

# DECISION 4: Which countries and years go into the all-country aggregate?
# Adding up researchers and employment across whichever countries happen to
# report in a given year would make the total jump whenever a country enters
# or leaves the data. So the aggregate uses a fixed (balanced) panel: only
# countries that report researchers in EVERY year from AGGREGATE_START to
# AGGREGATE_END. Nothing is interpolated. Countries that report only every
# other year (e.g. Sweden, Norway, Austria) drop out under this rule.
AGGREGATE_START = 1995
AGGREGATE_END = 2023

# DECISION 5: How to handle China's change of definition?
# China is about two-thirds of the panel's employment, so it dominates the
# pooled total. Before 2009, China counted researchers using the Frascati
# definition only in its independent research institutes; every other sector
# reported UNESCO "scientists and engineers", a broader group. From 2009 all
# sectors follow the Frascati Manual, and the OECD flags 2009 as a break in
# series. The 2008-to-2009 change in China's figure therefore mixes a change
# of definition with a year of real change.
#
# To put China's earlier years on the Frascati basis, we scale every pre-2009
# Chinese researcher count by one constant factor (a "level shift"). The size
# of the shift is the observed 2008-to-2009 log change MINUS the real growth
# China would plausibly have had that year. We take that real growth to be the
# average of China's log growth in the year before and the year after the
# break (2007-2008 and 2009-2010). Shifting by the whole observed change
# would instead assume China's research share did not grow at all in 2009.
BREAK_COUNTRY = "CHN"
BREAK_YEAR = 2009

# DECISION 6: How much to smooth the growth rate?
# Year-to-year growth is noisy (series breaks, recessions), so the growth chart
# also shows a Hodrick-Prescott trend. The HP filter needs a smoothing
# parameter; 6.25 is the standard choice for annual data (Ravn and Uhlig,
# 2002), equivalent to the familiar 1600 for quarterly data.
HP_SMOOTHING = 6.25









WarningData Processing Decision: comparing different latest years



Countries report on different schedules, so each country is shown at its own most recent year, and that year appears in the tooltip. A country is left out of the ranking if its latest figure is more than five years older than the newest year in the data (it is listed below the chart instead). A few countries have R&D personnel figures but no researcher figures, or the other way round, so the two views do not contain exactly the same countries.

md`**Left out as out of date:** ${stale.map(d => `${d.country} (latest: ${d[`${measure}_year`]}, ${d[`${measure}_per_1000`].toFixed(1)} per 1,000)`).join("; ") || "none"}.`
















Grey bars are the OECD and European Union aggregates. The top of the table is mostly Nordic countries and East Asian economies with strong manufacturing. Southern and Eastern European countries, Latin American members and South Africa sit at the bottom.






NoteCode: selecting each country’s latest value





def build_latest(timeseries) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    """Each country's most recent value for each ratio, with a staleness flag.

    The two ratios are treated separately: a country's latest researchers
    figure and latest R&D-personnel figure may come from different years, so
    each gets its own year column. The "*_is_current" columns apply DECISION 1.
    """
    newest_year = max(r["year"] for r in timeseries if r["researchers_per_1000"] != "")
    cutoff = newest_year - CURRENT_WINDOW_YEARS

    latest = {}
    for row in timeseries:  # rows are sorted by year, so later rows overwrite earlier
        entry = latest.setdefault(row["country_code"], {
            "country_code": row["country_code"],
            "country": row["country"],
            "is_aggregate": row["is_aggregate"],
            "researchers_year": "", "researchers_per_1000": "", "researchers_flags": "",
            "rd_personnel_year": "", "rd_personnel_per_1000": "", "rd_personnel_flags": "",
        })
        if row["researchers_per_1000"] != "":
            entry["researchers_year"] = row["year"]
            entry["researchers_per_1000"] = row["researchers_per_1000"]
            entry["researchers_flags"] = row["researchers_flags"]
        if row["rd_personnel_per_1000"] != "":
            entry["rd_personnel_year"] = row["year"]
            entry["rd_personnel_per_1000"] = row["rd_personnel_per_1000"]
            entry["rd_personnel_flags"] = row["rd_personnel_flags"]

    table = []
    for entry in latest.values():
        # Each ratio is judged on its own latest year.
        for prefix in ("researchers", "rd_personnel"):
            year = entry[f"{prefix}_year"]
            entry[f"{prefix}_is_current"] = year != "" and year > cutoff
        year = entry["researchers_year"]
        # Convert "per 1,000" to "percent of workforce" for plain-language text:
        # 17.8 per 1,000 = 1.78 per 100 = 1.78%.
        entry["researchers_pct_of_workforce"] = (
            round(entry["researchers_per_1000"] / 10, 3) if year != "" else ""
        )
        table.append(entry)
    # Highest first, which is the order the ranking chart uses.
    return sorted(table, key=lambda r: -(r["researchers_per_1000"] or 0))









ImportantIssue: many recent figures are provisional or defined differently



Look at the tooltips. Many 2024 figures carry the OECD flag provisional value, and a large number are flagged definition differs. That flag means a country’s survey departs from the Frascati guidelines in some documented way, for example in which sectors or fields it covers. The U.S. figure is flagged estimated. Differences of a few tenths between neighbouring countries are therefore not meaningful.



Which sectors employ the researchers?
This chart splits each country’s researchers into business, government and higher education (university) sectors. It uses each country’s latest year in which all three are reported. Countries are sorted by business share.


Show the sector chart code
sectorOrder = ["Business", "Government", "Higher education", "Other / unallocated"]
sectorColors = ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#c9c6bf"]
// Sort countries by the business share, highest first.
businessShare = new Map(sectors.filter(d => d.sector === "Business").map(d => [d.country, d.share_pct]))

Plot.plot({
  width,
  height: businessShare.size * 17 + 70,

  color: {domain: sectorOrder, range: sectorColors, legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(sectors, {
      x: "share_pct", y: "country", fill: "sector",
      order: sectorOrder,
      insetTop: 1.5, insetBottom: 1.5, insetLeft: 1,  // 1px gap between segments
      tip: true,
      title: d => [
        `${d.country} (${d.year})`,
        `${d.sector}: ${d.share_pct.toFixed(1)}% of researchers`,
        d.flags ? `Note: ${d.flags}` : ""
      ].filter(Boolean).join("\n")
    })
  ]
})




































NoteCode: calculating sector shares





SECTORS = {
    "B_RS": "Business",
    "G_RS": "Government",
    "H_RS": "Higher education",
}


def build_sector_shares(obs, labels, current_codes) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
    """Where each country's researchers work, in its latest year with all three sectors.

    The OECD publishes each sector's researchers as a percentage of the national
    total (unit PT_RSH). We use the most recent year in which ALL three sectors
    are reported, so the pieces come from the same year.

    The three sectors do not always add to 100%: the fourth Frascati sector,
    private non-profit institutions, is not in MSTI's researcher breakdown, and
    some countries report partial breakdowns. We show the remainder explicitly
    as "Other / unallocated" rather than rescaling the other three to fill it.
    """
    table = []
    for area in sorted(current_codes):
        years = [
            year for (a, measure, unit, year) in obs
            if a == area and measure == "B_RS" and unit == "PT_RSH"
        ]
        # Walk backwards from the newest year until all three sectors exist.
        for year in sorted(years, reverse=True):
            parts = {code: obs.get((area, code, "PT_RSH", year)) for code in SECTORS}
            if all(parts.values()):
                break
        else:
            continue  # this country never reports a complete breakdown

        remainder = 100 - sum(value(row) for row in parts.values())
        for code, sector in SECTORS.items():
            table.append({
                "country_code": area,
                "country": labels["CL_AREA"].get(area, area),
                "year": year,
                "sector": sector,
                "share_pct": round(value(parts[code]), 3),
                "flags": describe_flags(parts[code], labels),
            })
        table.append({
            "country_code": area,
            "country": labels["CL_AREA"].get(area, area),
            "year": year,
            "sector": "Other / unallocated",
            # Tiny negative remainders are rounding in the published shares.
            "share_pct": round(max(remainder, 0), 3),
            "flags": "Calculated by us as 100 minus the three published shares",
        })
    return table





Show how the numbers in this paragraph are computed
businessPct = code => sectors.find(d => d.country_code === code && d.sector === "Business").share_pct.toFixed(0)
md`The countries with the most researchers tend to be the ones where companies employ most of them. In South Korea, ${businessPct("KOR")}% of researchers work in business, and in the United States ${businessPct("USA")}%. Where the researcher share is low, universities usually employ most researchers. That is the pattern in Latvia, Lithuania, Croatia, Costa Rica and, most sharply, South Africa. In other words, a large research workforce mostly reflects how much R&D industry does.`
















The scatter plot below puts this relationship on a more formal footing. Each point is one country. The horizontal axis is the share of its researchers who work in business, and the vertical axis is its researchers per 1,000 employed. Both come from the same year: the latest year with a complete sector breakdown. The line is an ordinary least-squares fit, and the shaded band is its 95% confidence interval.

NoteCode: pairing each country’s business share with its researcher intensity, and fitting the line





def build_sector_fit(sectors, timeseries) -> tuple[list[dict[str, object]], dict[str, float]]:
    """Does a larger research workforce go with a larger business share?

    One point per country: the share of its researchers who work in business
    (x) against its researchers per 1,000 employed (y). Both come from the
    SAME year, the latest year with a complete sector breakdown, so the two
    numbers describe the same moment. Countries with no researcher ratio in
    that year are left out, and so are the OECD and EU totals (DECISION 2).

    The line is an ordinary least-squares fit, y = intercept + slope x.
    r is the correlation and r_squared the share of the cross-country
    variation in y that the line accounts for.
    """
    ratio = {(r["country_code"], r["year"]): r["researchers_per_1000"] for r in timeseries}
    points = []
    for row in sectors:
        if row["sector"] != "Business" or row["country_code"] in AGGREGATES:
            continue
        y = ratio.get((row["country_code"], row["year"]), "")
        if y == "":
            continue
        points.append({
            "country_code": row["country_code"],
            "country": row["country"],
            "year": row["year"],
            "business_share_pct": row["share_pct"],
            "researchers_per_1000": y,
        })

    n = len(points)
    xs = [p["business_share_pct"] for p in points]
    ys = [p["researchers_per_1000"] for p in points]
    mean_x, mean_y = sum(xs) / n, sum(ys) / n
    sxx = sum((x - mean_x) ** 2 for x in xs)
    syy = sum((y - mean_y) ** 2 for y in ys)
    sxy = sum((x - mean_x) * (y - mean_y) for x, y in zip(xs, ys))
    slope = sxy / sxx
    fit = {
        "n": n,
        "slope": slope,
        "intercept": mean_y - slope * mean_x,
        "r": sxy / math.sqrt(sxx * syy),
        "r_squared": sxy ** 2 / (sxx * syy),
    }
    return points, fit









ImportantIssue: the “other” slice



The Frascati Manual defines a fourth sector, private non-profit institutions, but MSTI does not publish its share of researchers. Some countries also report breakdowns that do not add up to their total. We show the leftover explicitly as Other / unallocated (100 minus the three published shares) instead of stretching the three sectors to fill 100%. It is largest for Chile and the United States. There it probably reflects the non-profit sector and revisions to the total that have not been carried into the breakdown, but MSTI does not say which.

title: Philosophy
text:
Checklist
I try to make sure every investigation contains the following:

A source ledger. Every dataset has a publisher, original URL, retrieval date, description, and license or terms link.
A preserved snapshot. The exact raw input used for publication is committed whenever its terms and size allow it. Large or restricted files receive a checksum and durable archive location instead.
A complete transformation path. Scripts convert raw inputs into analysis-ready files without undocumented manual edits.
Visible analytical choices. Definitions, exclusions, joins, missing-data treatment, and material assumptions are explained in ordinary language and code.
Reproducible outputs. A single documented command rebuilds derived data and the site.
Limitations and uncertainty. The article states what the evidence does not establish.


Evidence hierarchy
Primary government and institutional sources are preferred. Mirrors and aggregators may aid discovery, but the article should link to the originating publisher whenever possible. A source’s official status does not make it error-free; definitions, revisions, collection methods, and known limitations still require scrutiny.


Reproduction levels
Each article declares one of these levels:

Fully reproducible: all necessary inputs and code are included or openly downloadable.
Reproducible with external data: code is complete, but a documented download is required because data is too large to commit.
Partially reproducible: a legal, privacy, or access constraint prevents redistribution; the missing component and verification approach are stated prominently.
